questions.prompt: Engineers want to rebuild coastal wetlands near a city. Sort each item: is it a criterion (what success looks like) or a constraint (a limit the design must work within)?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Engineers want to rebuild coastal wetlands near a city. Sort each item as a criterion, meaning what success looks like, or a constraint, meaning a limit the design must work within. The items are: the marsh must be healthy enough to support fish and nesting birds; nearby neighborhoods suffer less damage from storms; budget: no more than the city can afford; the design must not cause extra flooding of homes; levees and buildings already take up much of the nearby low land.

items.text: The marsh must be healthy enough to support fish and nesting birds
items.rationale: It describes the outcome success is judged by, so it is a criterion.

items.text: Nearby neighborhoods suffer less damage from storms
items.rationale: Better storm protection is a goal of the wetland buffer, so it is a criterion.

items.text: Budget: no more than the city can afford
items.rationale: Budget is a limit on the design, so it is a constraint.

items.text: The design must not cause extra flooding of homes
items.rationale: Not flooding homes is a safety limit the design must stay within, so it is a constraint.

items.text: Levees and buildings already take up much of the nearby low land
items.rationale: Existing structures restrict where and how the design can be built, so it is a constraint.

questions.explanation: Criteria describe what a successful solution must achieve, such as healthy marsh and better storm protection. Constraints are limits such as cost, safety and the space available. A design that meets the criteria but breaks a constraint, like causing new floods, isn't acceptable.
questions.misconception: Criteria and constraints are the same thing: any requirement placed on a design.
questions.hint: Goals the design should reach are criteria; limits it must not cross are constraints.

evidence.supports: Criteria are the standards for judging success, such as restoring healthy wetlands; being too expensive or causing additional flooding are constraints.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Protecting Local Communities from Flooding
evidence.supports: Densely populated, low coastal land protected by levees limits which designs can be built.

questions.prompt: Two teams describe success for a marsh project. Team 1: "Make the coast better." Team 2: "Within ten years, healthy marsh covers most of the project area." Why is Team 2's version more useful?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Two teams describe success for a marsh project. Team 1 writes: make the coast better. Team 2 writes: within ten years, healthy marsh covers most of the project area. Why is Team 2's version more useful?

choices.text: It can be measured, so the team can check whether the design worked
choices.rationale: Right. A marsh target with a deadline can be checked, so engineers can tell whether a design succeeded.

choices.text: It is longer, so it must include more science and more detail
choices.rationale: Length isn't the point. Team 1's goal is too vague to check, while Team 2's names what to measure and by when.

choices.text: It guarantees that the whole project will stay within the city's budget
choices.rationale: Cost is a constraint, and Team 2's statement says nothing about money.

choices.text: It means the design won't need any testing once it is built
choices.rationale: A precise criterion is what makes testing possible; it doesn't replace testing.

questions.explanation: A criterion is most useful when it is precise enough to check. "Make the coast better" can't be measured, but a marsh target with a deadline can, so engineers can compare designs and test results against it.
questions.misconception: Any goal statement works as a criterion, however vague.
questions.hint: Ten years from now, how would each team know whether it had succeeded?

evidence.supports: The more precisely a design task's criteria and constraints are defined, the more likely the designed solution is to succeed.
Solving a complex problem includes setting the criteria precisely; criteria are the standards a solution's success is judged by, such as restoring healthy wetlands.

questions.prompt: Near New Orleans, a gated diversion can let Mississippi River water through a levee into nearby marshes. Which way of running the gates best meets both the wetland criterion and the flood-safety constraint?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Near New Orleans, a gated diversion can let Mississippi River water through a levee into nearby marshes. Which way of running the gates best meets both the wetland criterion and the flood-safety constraint?

choices.text: Open when floods aren't a risk so river water feeds the marsh; close when they are
choices.rationale: Right. Opening serves the wetland criterion, and closing respects the flood-safety constraint.

choices.text: Stay open all year, so the marsh gets as much river water as possible
choices.rationale: Ignoring flood risk would break a key constraint, and nearby neighborhoods could flood.

choices.text: Stay closed all year, so neighborhoods are never at risk from river water
choices.rationale: Then little river water or sediment would reach the marsh, so the wetland criterion wouldn't be met.

choices.text: Open them wide during coastal storm floods, then close them again once the weather is calm
choices.rationale: This reverses the safe timing: river water added during a storm flood could reach neighborhoods, and closing in calm weather keeps sediment from the marsh.

questions.explanation: A good design balances criteria and constraints. The gates let river water and sediment feed the wetland when conditions are safe, which supports the marsh, and they close when high water threatens, which respects the limit of not flooding neighborhoods. Operators also adjust the gates for other reasons, such as salt water in the river.
questions.misconception: A design can satisfy only one goal, so engineers must pick either the environment or safety.
questions.hint: When would letting river water in be dangerous?

evidence.locator: Section 4, Protecting Local Communities from Flooding

questions.prompt: An open channel dug off the Atchafalaya River built new wetlands at Wax Lake, but engineers chose a gated diversion for crowded, low-lying land near New Orleans. What is the best lesson from this comparison?
questions.accessiblePrompt: An open channel dug off the Atchafalaya River built new wetlands at Wax Lake, but engineers chose a gated diversion for crowded, low-lying land near New Orleans. What is the best lesson from this comparison?

choices.text: The best design depends on local conditions and constraints
choices.rationale: Right. Each site's people, land and flood risks shape which design is safe and effective.

choices.text: A design that worked once should be copied to every coastline
choices.rationale: A design that works in one place can be unsafe in another, such as an open channel next to crowded neighborhoods.

choices.text: Gates were chosen near New Orleans mainly because they cost less to build
choices.rationale: The lesson's reason is flood risk to crowded, low-lying neighborhoods, not lower cost.

choices.text: Wax Lake's channel stopped working, so engineers switched to gates
choices.rationale: The Wax Lake channel has kept building land for decades. The New Orleans design differs because local conditions differ.

questions.explanation: Wax Lake's open channel worked where it led away from towns into an open bay, while near New Orleans a permanent opening could flood homes, so engineers built gates they can close. Engineers fit each solution to the criteria and constraints of its location.
questions.misconception: A solution that works in one place will work the same way everywhere.
questions.hint: What was different about the land around New Orleans?

questions.prompt: One scientific estimate says that two young river deltas in Atchafalaya Bay, Louisiana, together gain about 2.8 km² of new land per year on average. At that average rate, how many years would it take them to add 14 km²?
questions.accessiblePrompt: One scientific estimate says that two young river deltas in Atchafalaya Bay, Louisiana, together gain about 2.8 square kilometers of new land per year on average. At that average rate, how many years would it take them to add 14 square kilometers?
questions.workedSolution: Time = total new land ÷ new land per year = 14 km² ÷ 2.8 km² per year = 5 years.
questions.conditions: Assume the average rate stays the same every year.
questions.limitations: Real delta growth varies a lot from year to year with floods and hurricanes; this is an average-rate estimate.
questions.explanation: Dividing the total area by the yearly rate gives the time: 14 ÷ 2.8 = 5 years. Real deltas don't grow evenly; big floods deliver extra sediment and hurricanes can wash land away, so this is only an average-rate estimate.
questions.misconception: To find the time from a rate, you multiply the total by the rate.
questions.hint: How many groups of 2.8 fit into 14?

evidence.supports: After the diversion channel was dug, new wetlands formed at about 2.8 square kilometers per year.

evidence.title: New Land on the Louisiana Coast
evidence.supports: One estimate by Louisiana State University scientists, reported by NASA, says the Atchafalaya and Wax Lake Outlet deltas have combined to grow about 2.8 square kilometers per year; the Wax Lake delta alone grows about 1.2. The page does not say the estimate came from satellite studies.

evidence.title: World of Change: Growing Deltas in Atchafalaya Bay
evidence.supports: The deltas' growth rate has varied considerably with the timing of major floods and hurricanes.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a river can build new coastal wetland.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Put these steps in order, from first to last, to show how a river can build new coastal wetland. The steps are: wetland plants such as reeds and willows take root on the highest new ground; the river picks up sand and mud from land far upstream; the growing marsh helps buffer nearby towns from storm surges; sediment settles in the shallow bay and builds sandbars and low islands; muddy river water flows out into a shallow coastal bay.

items.text: Wetland plants such as reeds and willows take root on the highest new ground
items.rationale: Plants can colonize only after sediment has built land above the water.

items.text: The river picks up sand and mud from land far upstream
items.rationale: Everything starts with the river carrying sediment from far away.

items.text: The growing marsh helps buffer nearby towns from storm surges
items.rationale: Only an established marsh can soften storms, so this comes last.

items.text: Sediment settles in the shallow bay and builds sandbars and low islands
items.rationale: Once in shallow water, sediment settles out and piles up into new land.

items.text: Muddy river water flows out into a shallow coastal bay
items.rationale: The sediment-filled water must reach the coast before it can settle there.

questions.limitations: This is a simplified sequence; in real deltas, floods, storms and tides keep adding and removing sediment at the same time.
questions.explanation: Wetlands grow from the ground up: a river carries sediment to the coast, the sediment settles in shallow water and builds new land, plants colonize it and their roots hold it in place, and the marsh then helps protect nearby communities. Cut off the sediment and the process stops.
questions.misconception: Coastal wetlands are permanent and don't need a supply of river sediment.
questions.hint: Land has to exist before plants can grow on it.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Rebuilding Wetland Buffers and Figure 4 (rendered)
evidence.supports: The river carries sediment from far away and deposits it where it enters the Gulf, forming wetlands; wetland plants grow on new islands, and healthy wetlands protect communities from storms.

evidence.title: World of Change: Growing Deltas in Atchafalaya Bay
evidence.supports: Sediment carried by the Atchafalaya River settles into shallow water; reeds and willows colonize the higher sandbars, and their roots stabilize the sediment.

review.notes: Drafted from rendered p. 292 plus NASA. Only one order is defensible: land must form before plants, and the buffer comes from the grown marsh. questions.prompt: Many coastal wetlands near New Orleans have been shrinking. Based on the lesson, what is one important reason?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Many coastal wetlands near New Orleans have been shrinking. Based on the lesson, what is one important reason?

choices.text: Levees and a changed river path keep sediment from reaching them
choices.rationale: Right. Without new sediment, the marshes can't rebuild what they lose.

choices.text: The river now dumps far too much sediment and buries the marsh
choices.rationale: The problem near New Orleans is too little sediment reaching the marshes, not too much.

choices.text: The marshes are slowly filling in and turning into forest through succession
choices.rationale: Filling in would turn marsh into drier land, not shrink it; the lesson ties the loss of these marshes to river sediment that no longer reaches them.

choices.text: Wetland plants slowly use up the soil until nothing is left
choices.rationale: Plant roots actually help hold soil in place; plants don't consume the land.

questions.explanation: Left alone, the Mississippi River spreads sediment that builds and refreshes coastal wetlands. Levees and a changed river path keep much of that sediment from reaching some marshes, so they can't keep up and they shrink. Diversions try to reconnect wetlands to river sediment.
questions.misconception: Wetlands stay the same size on their own without a fresh supply of sediment.
questions.hint: What did the river deliver to the coast before levees were built?

evidence.supports: The Mississippi River naturally deposits sediment that forms coastal wetlands, but people changed the river's path and some places no longer receive sediment.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Protecting Local Communities from Flooding
evidence.supports: Levees prevent the natural flow of water and sediment that builds wetlands.

questions.prompt: Ecosystem changes can start in nature or with people. Sort each change by what set it off: natural, or caused by people.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Ecosystem changes can start in nature or with people. Sort each change by what set it off: natural, or caused by people. The changes are: a hurricane's winds flatten a coastal forest; heavy rain loosens a steep slope, and a landslide buries a meadow; a long drought dries up a prairie pond; a tanker leaks oil into a coastal bay; farmers plow up a prairie to plant wheat; someone releases a new kind of fish into a lake where it never lived; and weed seeds stuck to hikers' boots sprout in a park far from home.

items.text: A hurricane's winds flatten a coastal forest
items.rationale: Hurricanes are storms that form over warm ocean water; no person sets them off.

items.text: Heavy rain loosens a steep slope, and a landslide buries a meadow
items.rationale: Rain and gravity set off this landslide, so it is a natural change.

items.text: A long drought dries up a prairie pond
items.rationale: A drought is a natural weather pattern, even though it can badly harm an ecosystem.

items.text: A tanker leaks oil into a coastal bay
items.rationale: The oil came from a ship people built and run, so people caused this change.

items.text: Farmers plow up a prairie to plant wheat
items.rationale: Clearing land for farming is a human activity.

items.text: Someone releases a new kind of fish into a lake where it never lived
items.rationale: A person moved this species on purpose, so it is an introduced species.

items.text: Weed seeds stuck to hikers' boots sprout in a park far from home
items.rationale: People carried these seeds by accident. A human-caused change doesn't have to be on purpose.

questions.limitations: Human activity can make some natural events, such as droughts, more likely or more severe; this sort asks only what directly set off each change. Wildfires are left out because they can start either way.
questions.explanation: Hurricanes, landslides and droughts are natural events. Oil spills, clearing land and moving species into new places are caused by people, whether on purpose or by accident. Both kinds of change can disrupt an ecosystem for a short time or for good.
questions.misconception: A change counts as caused by people only when someone does it on purpose.
questions.hint: Trace each change back to its starting point. Was a person's action part of how it began?

evidence.supports: Eruptions, hurricanes, droughts, fires, landslides and floods are natural events; people also change ecosystems suddenly by clearing land, causing oil spills and other pollution, and bringing new species into an area, sometimes by accident.
Ecosystems change naturally, as when an avalanche destroys a hillside of trees, and because of people, as when a forest is cleared for a field.

evidence.title: introduced species (NAL Thesaurus concept)
evidence.supports: Introduced species are species brought by humans, intentionally or unintentionally, into a new geographic area outside their native range.

questions.prompt: Engineers open a river diversion to rebuild a shrinking marsh. Which evidence would best show that the diversion is really building new marsh?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Engineers open a river diversion to rebuild a shrinking marsh. Which evidence would best show that the diversion is really building new marsh?

choices.text: Satellite measurements taken every year, compared with a similar marsh with no diversion
choices.rationale: Right. Measurements repeated over many years show a trend, and the comparison marsh shows what would have happened without the diversion.

choices.text: A single photo of bright green marsh near the gates, taken after one especially wet spring
choices.rationale: One photo from one season can't show a long-term trend; marshes look greener in some seasons and years than in others.

choices.text: The project's design plan, which says that new marsh should form there within ten years
choices.rationale: A plan states a goal; it isn't evidence that the goal was met.

choices.text: A news story in which local leaders say the project has been a great success so far
choices.rationale: Praise is an opinion; it doesn't measure how much marsh formed.

questions.limitations: Real monitoring also uses ground surveys, and no two marshes are exactly alike, so a comparison marsh is matched as closely as possible.
questions.explanation: Strong evidence that a restoration works comes from measurements repeated over many years and compared with a similar place that got no help. Engineers keep collecting data after a project is built, because a stated goal or one hopeful photo can't show whether new land is really forming.
questions.misconception: A stated goal or one good-looking result proves that a design works.
questions.hint: Which evidence could tell a real, lasting change apart from a lucky season or a hopeful claim?
